claims.claim: Janschewitz (2008) normed 460 English words (92 of them taboo) on seven dimensions: personal use, familiarity, offensiveness, tabooness, valence, arousal and imageability. Each was rated on a 1-9 scale, with 9 the highest. The design separates the rater's own reaction from their view of society's reaction. Offensiveness is how personally offensive the rater finds the word. Tabooness is how offensive the rater thinks it is to people in general. All word sets were rated higher on familiarity and tabooness than on personal use and offensiveness, and the gap was largest for the taboo set.
claims.source: Janschewitz, K. (2008). Taboo, emotionally valenced, and emotionally neutral word norms. Behavior Research Methods, 40(4), 1065-1074.
claims.population: 78 US college students, English L1 (mostly). The count of 460 words with 92 taboo comes from a secondary source.
claims.scale: 1-9 for each dimension, 9 the highest. Only valence is reported to have a neutral midpoint (5). I could not confirm the exact anchors for offensiveness and tabooness.
claims.relevance: This is the main English norm set. Its split between personal offence and offence to people in general suits a learner app: rate how society hears the word, not how one rater feels. A 9-point scale is too fine to show on a card, so it would be collapsed into bands.

claims.claim: Dewaele (2004) surveyed 1,039 multilinguals through the Bilingualism and Emotions Questionnaire, rating each of up to five languages. The perceived emotional force of swearwords and taboo words is highest in the L1 and lower in each language learned after it. People who learned a language naturalistically gave higher ratings than classroom learners. Self-rated proficiency and frequency of use predicted the ratings. Age of onset of learning predicted them only for the L2. Self-reported L1 attriters rated their L1 words as weaker. Women gave higher ratings than men.
claims.source: Dewaele, J.-M. (2004). The emotional force of swearwords and taboo words in the speech of multilinguals. Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development, 25(2/3), 204-222.
claims.population: 1,039 adult multilinguals with many L1s, from an online survey. Ratings were given per language (L1 to L5).
claims.scale: Five-point Likert scale for the question 'Do swear and taboo words in your different languages have the same emotional weight for you?' (1/does not feel strong, 2/little, 3/fairly, 4/strong, 5/very strong)
claims.relevance: English-speaking learners of Bengali, Hindi or Spanish will feel these words much less strongly than native speakers do. So each card's level should state the native speaker's judgement, not how strong the word feels to the learner. This is the basis for the app's 'never use one by mistake' aim.

claims.claim: Dewaele (2016) asked 1,159 L1 and 1,165 LX (foreign-language) users of English to judge 30 negative emotion-laden words from the British National Corpus. The words ranged from mildly to extremely negative. LX users rated most words as more offensive than L1 users did, except the single most offensive word, which they underrated. They were less sure of exact meanings and said they avoid the most offensive words. Dewaele suggests classroom warnings attach a 'red flag' that makes learners overestimate. Differences among LX users were linked to living in an English-speaking environment, how they acquired English, and their proficiency.
claims.source: Dewaele, J.-M. (2016). Thirty shades of offensiveness: L1 and LX English users' understanding, perception and self-reported use of negative emotion-laden words. Journal of Pragmatics, 94, 112-127.
claims.population: English. 1,159 L1 and 1,165 LX users from many countries, online questionnaire.
claims.scale: Offensiveness rating per word. I could not confirm the number of points or the anchors (the full text is at eprints.bbk.ac.uk/14482).
claims.relevance: Learners misjudge the words at both ends: they overrate mid-level words and underrate the strongest. A card can correct this by showing an explicit native-speaker level and singling out the top band ('strongest').

claims.claim: Sulpizio, Günther, ... Marelli (2024) built a cross-language database of taboo words. Study 1 collected taboo words (N = 1046). Study 2 collected ratings on six dimensions (N = 455 per dimension) across 13 languages and 17 countries, including Spanish samples from Spain and Chile. Offensiveness was defined as how offensive the rater personally finds the word. Tabooness was defined as the extent to which it is not acceptable to use the word in most social situations. Ratings used best-worst scaling, not a fixed point scale. Reliabilities for valence, tabooness and offensiveness were high (r > .80) in most samples. Tabooness and offensiveness varied significantly from country to country. The most taboo or offensive words were almost exclusively about female genitalia or female family members. Words about mental or physical disability ranked among the most offensive in most languages.
claims.source: Sulpizio, S., Günther, F., Badan, L., Basclain, B., Brysbaert, M., ... Marelli, M. (2024). Taboo language across the globe: A multi-lab study. Behavior Research Methods, 56, 3794-3813.
claims.population: Native speakers of 13 languages in 17 countries, including Spain and Chile. As far as I found, no Indian language is included.
claims.scale: Best-worst scaling: each trial shows N items and the rater picks the highest and the lowest, which gives continuous scores. No Likert points.
claims.relevance: This is the only large study I found with Spanish offensiveness data, and it has separate samples for Spain and Chile. Because offensiveness differs by country, a Spanish card's level may need a region note. The pattern of insults aimed at female relatives matches common Hindi and Bengali insults (for example 'behenchod'), but that comparison is my inference.

claims.claim: The Dutch Taboo Norms rate 672 Dutch words, 202 of them taboo, for general taboo, personal taboo, insult, valence and arousal. Ratings used a 7-point Likert scale. Split-half reliabilities were high. The authors noted that before their study, tabooness norms existed only for English.
claims.source: Roest, S. A., Visser, T. A., & Zeelenberg, R. (2018; online 2017). Dutch taboo norms. Behavior Research Methods, 50, 630-641.
claims.population: 87 Dutch psychology students (58 female, 29 male) at Erasmus University Rotterdam, Dutch L1.
claims.scale: 7-point Likert. I could not confirm the anchor labels.
claims.relevance: This is a second model for norming taboo words in a new language. It rates general (societal) taboo separately from personal taboo, as Janschewitz does. It also adds an 'insult' dimension, which could help the app label words that are used as insults.

claims.claim: In Beers Fägersten's 2007 study, University of Florida undergraduates rated swear words for offensiveness on a 1-10 scale, both on their own and inside short dialogues. Words in context were rated less offensive than the same words alone (also reported by Mormol 2018). Sexual swear words ranked as more offensive than religious ones in both tasks. Perceived offensiveness depended on the dialogue and on the raters' gender and race.
claims.source: Beers Fägersten, K. (2007). A sociolinguistic analysis of swear word offensiveness. Saarland Working Papers in Linguistics, 1, 14-37.
claims.population: US undergraduates (University of Florida), English L1, of mixed gender and race.
claims.scale: Offensiveness from 1 to 10, '1' being 'Not Offensive', and '10' being 'Very Offensive'
claims.relevance: A single level per word is a simplification, because context changes offensiveness. Cards could carry a short context note. It also shows that the semantic category of a word (sexual vs religious) predicts its rank.

claims.claim: Jay and Janschewitz (2008) had native and non-native English-speaking college students rate how offensive and how likely hypothetical swearing scenarios were. They argue that the emotional impact of swearing depends on experience with a culture and its language conventions. Secondary sources summarise the paper as showing that acceptability depends on the speaker's social position, gender and age, and on the setting and the relationship with the listener.
claims.source: Jay, T., & Janschewitz, K. (2008). The pragmatics of swearing. Journal of Politeness Research, 4(2), 267-288.
claims.population: US college students, native and non-native English speakers.
claims.scale: Not confirmed. Offensiveness and likelihood ratings of scenarios that vary speaker, listener and setting.
claims.relevance: This supports adding a 'who and where' note to cards. The level of a word depends on who says it to whom, so the app can teach recognition by context.

claims.claim: Jay (2009) reports that a set of 10 words, stable for the past 20 years, accounts for 80% of public swearing in American English recordings. Swearing correlates positively with extraversion and Type A hostility and negatively with agreeableness, conscientiousness, religiosity and sexual anxiety. Taboo words carry emotional information (anger, frustration) more readily than non-taboo words.
claims.source: Jay, T. (2009). The utility and ubiquity of taboo words. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 4(2), 153-161.
claims.population: American English. Public recordings plus a review of laboratory research.
claims.scale: None. Frequency and review data, no rating scale.
claims.relevance: A small core vocabulary covers most real swearing, so a recognition deck can be short and still cover most of what a learner will hear. A frequency field next to the level would help choose which words to teach first.

claims.claim: Jay's book 'Cursing in America' (1992) has a chapter, 'The Offensiveness of Words: Sex and Semantics' (pp. 159-194). Per the publisher, the book includes word-by-word tables of degree of offensiveness and of the gender and age of speakers.
claims.source: Jay, T. (1992). Cursing in America. John Benjamins.
claims.scale: Not found.
claims.relevance: This is the earliest word-level offensiveness data for English. I did not find the scale it uses.

claims.claim: I found no published human-rated offensiveness or tabooness norms for Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati or Assamese. The existing resources are computational: Hindi-English code-mixed swear-word frequency lists, Hindi offensive-tweet datasets, and the Marathi MOLD dataset (about 2,500 tweets, found using 22 Marathi curse words as search terms and labelled offensive or not). A Kapoor (2016) study with Indian participants rating taboo words is cited, but I could not see its findings.
claims.source: Search finding. Example: Gaikwad, S. et al. (2021). Cross-lingual Offensive Language Identification for Low Resource Languages: The Case of Marathi. arXiv:2109.03552.
claims.scale: MOLD labels each tweet offensive or not offensive (binary). No graded human scale was found.
claims.relevance: Levels for the Indian-language cards will have to be set by the app's own native-speaker judges, not taken from published norms. The first step would be to run a small rating with a published scale (for example Janschewitz's 'to people in general' tabooness question) with native speakers.

claims.claim: Spanish has no dedicated taboo-word offensiveness norms that I could find. General affective norms exist: MADS (875 words rated by 540 Spanish native speakers for dominance, familiarity, age of acquisition and sensory experience) and a Mexican Spanish ANEW adaptation that found regional differences in arousal ratings. Neither covers swearwords. RAE dictionary labels (for example 'malsonante') and ASALE's Diccionario de americanismos labels ('vulg.', 'desp.', with the country of use) are the standard labels in practice.
claims.source: Search finding. MADS: Hinojosa, J. A. et al. (2016), Madrid Affective Database for Spanish, PLoS ONE (PMC4882010). The Sulpizio et al. (2024) Spain/Chile samples are the only Spanish offensiveness data found.
claims.scale: No offensiveness scale. RAE and ASALE use categorical register labels.
claims.relevance: For Spanish, combine the Sulpizio et al. (2024) Spain/Chile data with RAE/ASALE labels and a regional note. The same word can be mild in one country and strong in another (for example 'boludo'; this comes from popular guides, not research).

gaps: WebFetch could not resolve any host (DNS failure), so I read no abstract or full text directly. Every claim comes from search-engine summaries of abstracts and snippets. That is why none is rated High.

Janschewitz 2008: I could not confirm the anchor labels for the offensiveness and tabooness scales (only that they run 1-9 with 9 highest). The total of 460 words with 92 taboo comes from a secondary source.
Dewaele 2016 (Thirty shades): I did not find the offensiveness scale's number of points or anchors, or the per-word means.
Sulpizio et al. 2024: I did not confirm the full list of 13 languages or whether any Indian language is included. I did not find the per-word Spanish data (supplementary materials / OSF).
Beers Fägersten 2012 (book 'Who's Swearing Now?'): I did not confirm its method. Only the 2007 working paper's 1-10 scale was found.
Jay 1992 Cursing in America: I did not find its offensiveness scale.
There are no published offensiveness norms for any of the app's Indian languages. Kapoor 2016 (Indian participants rating taboo words) is cited but unverified.

The user asked for two separate similarity matrices: words that sound similar to offensive words and words written similarly. I found no research on phonological or orthographic similarity to taboo words, such as studies of near-homophones of swearwords. This needs a separate search.

Overall pattern, my own inference: research norms use fine scales (5, 7, 9 or 10 points, or best-worst scaling) for research purposes. For display, a 4-band scale like Ofcom's (mild / medium / strong / strongest), set from native-speaker judgement of how 'people in general' would react, matches both Janschewitz's tabooness concept and Dewaele's finding that L2 users misjudge strength.

checked.claim: Janschewitz (2008): 460 English words (92 taboo), seven dimensions (personal use, familiarity, offensiveness, tabooness, valence, arousal, imageability), 1-9 scales; personal reaction separated from perceived societal reaction; familiarity and tabooness rated higher than personal use and offensiveness, gap largest for taboo set.
checked.source: Janschewitz, K. (2008). Taboo, emotionally valenced, and emotionally neutral word norms. Behavior Research Methods, 40(4), 1065-1074. https://doi.org/10.3758/BRM.40.4.1065 (PubMed 19001397)
checked.correction: Confirmed via abstract snippets and secondary sources only (WebFetch could not reach publisher/PubMed in this environment; DNS failures). 78 US undergraduates, 460 words, 92 taboo: secondary. Abstract says frequency and inappropriateness measures were split into personal reactions (personal use, offensiveness) vs perceived societal reactions (familiarity, tabooness); the familiarity/tabooness > personal use/offensiveness gap, largest for taboo set, appears in abstract-derived text. 9-point scale confirmed for tabooness by a citing norming study, which quotes Janschewitz's tabooness instruction as "How offensive the word is to people in general?"; offensiveness = personally upsetting/offensive (secondary, 2023 citing paper). One citing paper notes only 52 of the 92 pre-assigned taboo words were rated >= 4.5 on tabooness, which matters if reusing the set. Anchors for every dimension not confirmed. Keep confidence Medium.

checked.claim: Dewaele (2004): 1,039 multilinguals via Bilingualism and Emotions web questionnaire; emotional force of swear/taboo words highest in L1, lower in later languages; naturalistic learners higher than instructed; proficiency and frequency of use predict; age of onset only for L2; L1 attriters rate L1 weaker; women higher than men. Five-point Likert with anchors 1 does not feel strong ... 5 very strong.
checked.source: Dewaele, J.-M. (2004). Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development, 25(2-3), 204-222. https://doi.org/10.1080/01434630408666529 ; preprint eprints.bbk.ac.uk/62/1/dewaeleJMMD25.pdf
checked.correction: Bibliographic details, N = 1,039, the L1 > later-language gradient, naturalistic > instructed, proficiency and frequency of use as predictors, age of onset only for L2 (per CORE abstract listing), and weaker ratings by L1 attriters are confirmed from abstract text. The question wording 'Do swear and taboo words in your different languages have the same emotional weight for you?' with five-point Likert, repeated for up to five languages, is confirmed. NOT confirmed: the anchor labels (1 'does not feel strong' ... 5 'very strong'); remove them or mark unverified. Gender: only a truncated snippet ('female participants consistently rated the emotional force of S-T words higher than males, particularly in ...') and a figure 'Effect of gender on perceived emotional force of swearwords in five languages'. Direction is supported, but scope (which languages) is unconfirmed.

checked.claim: Dewaele (2016): 1,159 L1 and 1,165 LX English users judged 30 negative emotion-laden words from the BNC (mildly to extremely negative); LX users rated most words more offensive except the most offensive word; less sure of meanings; avoid most offensive words; 'red flag' classroom warnings; LX variation linked to living in English-speaking environment, context of acquisition, proficiency.
checked.source: Dewaele, J.-M. (2016). Thirty shades of offensiveness. Journal of Pragmatics, 94, 112-127. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pragma.2016.01.009 ; preprint eprints.bbk.ac.uk/id/eprint/14482/3/14482.pdf
checked.correction: All points match the abstract as returned by search, with one wording fix. The abstract does not say LX users 'avoid the most offensive words'. It says LX users reported more frequent use of relatively less offensive words, while L1 users reported more use of the more taboo words. The 'red flag' idea is in the abstract: learners are warned about such words and attach a red flag reminding them of their power. The rating scale points and anchors are still unconfirmed.

checked.claim: Sulpizio, Günther, ... Marelli (2024): Study 1 N = 1046; Study 2 six dimensions N = 455 each; 13 languages, 17 countries incl. Spain and Chile; best-worst scaling; offensiveness = personal, tabooness = 'not acceptable to use in most social situations'; reliabilities r > .80 for valence, tabooness, offensiveness in most samples; significant cross-country variability; most taboo/offensive words almost exclusively female genitalia or female family members; disability words among most offensive in most languages.
checked.source: Sulpizio, S., Günther, F., et al. (2024). Taboo language across the globe: A multi-lab study. Behavior Research Methods, 56(4), 3794-3813. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02376-6 (PMC11133054; HAL hal-04572180)
checked.correction: Confirmed: venue/volume/pages, N = 1046 (Study 1), N = 455 per dimension (Study 2), 13 languages and 17 countries, Spanish samples from Chile and Spain, best-worst scaling, six dimensions (AoA, concreteness, valence, arousal, offensiveness, tabooness), split-half reliabilities r > .80 for AoA, valence, tabooness and offensiveness in most samples (the claim omits AoA), significant cross-country variability, and the most taboo/offensive list being almost exclusively words about female genitalia or female family members. Also found: maricón is similarly taboo in Spain and Chile but more offensive in Spain, and puto is more offensive in Chile. This supports the region-note idea. NOT confirmed: (a) the exact tabooness wording 'not acceptable to use in most social situations'; the paraphrase found is that offensiveness is how a person perceives a word as inappropriate and tabooness is how a person believes society considers it inappropriate; (b) disability-related words ranking among the most offensive in most languages; (c) the co-author names 'Badan, Basclain, Brysbaert'. Cite as 'Sulpizio, Günther, et al.' unless checked.

checked.claim: Dutch Taboo Norms: 672 Dutch words, 202 taboo, rated on general taboo, personal taboo, insult, valence, arousal; 7-point scale; high split-half reliability; tabooness norms previously only for English. 87 Erasmus University Rotterdam psychology students (58 F, 29 M).
checked.source: Roest, S. A., Visser, T. A., & Zeelenberg, R. (2018). Dutch taboo norms. Behavior Research Methods, 50(2), 630-641 (online April 2017). https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0890-x (PMC5880853)
checked.correction: All stated facts confirmed from abstract-level search results, including the authors' statement that no tabooness norms had been collected in languages other than English. The issue is 50(2). Extra findings: many sex-related words scored high on taboo but low on insult, and some sex-related words scored high on both taboo and valence. Anchor labels not confirmed.

checked.claim: Beers Fägersten (2007): University of Florida undergraduates rated swear words 1-10 ('1' Not Offensive, '10' Very Offensive) in isolation and in dialogues; context lowered offensiveness (also Mormol 2018); sexual > religious in both tasks; offensiveness depended on dialogue and on raters' gender and race.
checked.source: Beers Fägersten, K. (2007). A sociolinguistic analysis of swear word offensiveness. Saarland Working Papers in Linguistics, 1, 14-37. https://publikationen.sulb.uni-saarland.de/bitstream/20.500.11880/23550/1/Beers_Faegersten.pdf
checked.correction: Confirmed: University of Florida undergraduates (N = 60 questionnaires: 33 male, 27 female; 23 also interviewed), the 1-10 scale with '1' being 'Not Offensive' and '10' being 'Very Offensive', a word-list task plus six recorded campus dialogues, and sexual terms rated above excretory and sacred terms. The finding that words in context were rated less offensive is attributed by a secondary source to Beers Fägersten (2012) and Mormol (2018), not only to the 2007 paper. Gender fix: in the word-list task, women's averages were consistently higher, but the difference was not significant (one-way ANOVA p = 0.0707). Race differences were significant in the dialogue task among males (p < 0.0001). Subgroups were very small. For example, one of seven African-American women rated every word 10. Sample word-list means: n-word 8.5, cunt 6.6, motherfucker 5.9, bitch 5.0, hell 2.3, damn 2.3.

checked.claim: Jay & Janschewitz (2008): native and non-native English-speaking college students rated offensiveness and likelihood of hypothetical swearing scenarios; emotional impact depends on cultural/linguistic experience; acceptability depends on speaker, setting, relationship.
checked.source: Jay, T., & Janschewitz, K. (2008). The pragmatics of swearing. Journal of Politeness Research, 4(2), 267-288. https://doi.org/10.1515/JPLR.2008.013 (author PDF at mcla.edu)
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the design (native and non-native college students rated the offensiveness and likelihood of scenarios). It also says appropriateness of swearing is highly contextually variable, depending on speaker-listener relationship, social-physical context and the particular word. Offensiveness ratings depended on gender for native speakers and on English experience for non-native speakers. The context dependence is in the abstract itself, not only in secondary summaries. Rating scale points still unconfirmed.

checked.claim: Jay (2009): 10 words stable over 20 years account for 80% of public swearing; swearing correlates positively with extraversion and Type A hostility, negatively with agreeableness, conscientiousness, religiosity, sexual anxiety; taboo words carry emotional information more readily.
checked.source: Jay, T. (2009). The utility and ubiquity of taboo words. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 4(2), 153-161. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-6924.2009.01115.x (PubMed 26158942; full text people.uncw.edu/hakanr/documents/useoftaboowords.pdf)
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the 10 words, the 80% figure, the 20-year stability and the personality correlations. Frequency counts are from 1986, 1997 and 2006. The emotional-information point is consistent with the abstract, but this check did not see it verbatim.

checked.claim: Jay (1992) Cursing in America has chapter 'The Offensiveness of Words: Sex and Semantics' (pp. 159-194); publisher says the book includes word-by-word tables of offensiveness and speaker gender/age.
checked.source: Jay, T. (1992). Cursing in America: A psycholinguistic study of dirty language in the courts, in the movies, in the schoolyards and on the streets. John Benjamins. https://doi.org/10.1075/z.57
checked.correction: Confirmed: the book, the publisher (John Benjamins, 1992, DOI 10.1075/z.57), and Chapter 5 'The Offensiveness of Words: Sex and Semantics' (with a subsection 'Offensiveness versus Offendedness'). The book is described as containing many word-by-word tables of frequency, offensiveness and speaker gender/age. NOT confirmed: the page range 159-194 and the chapter DOI 10.1075/z.57.05the. Cite the book DOI unless these are checked.

checked.claim: No published human-rated offensiveness/tabooness norms for Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati, Assamese; resources are computational (e.g., MOLD, about 2,500 tweets from 22 Marathi curse words, binary labels); Kapoor (2016) with Indian participants cited but findings unseen.
checked.source: Gaikwad, S., Ranasinghe, T., Zampieri, M., & Homan, C. (2021). Cross-lingual Offensive Language Identification for Low Resource Languages: The Case of Marathi. RANLP 2021, 437-443; arXiv:2109.03552. Kapoor, H. (2016). Swears in context: The difference between casual and abusive swearing. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-014-9345-z (PubMed 25480107)
checked.correction: MOLD confirmed: 2,499 tweets after cleaning (about 2,547 collected), collected by searching 22 common Marathi curse words. Non-offensive tweets came from politics, entertainment and sports searches with #Marathi. Six native annotators labelled each tweet OFF or NOT (binary). Published at RANLP 2021, pp. 437-443. Kapoor's findings are now findable. Its 254 participants (103 Indian, 151 non-Indian) rated how appropriate mild, moderate and severe swears are in casual and abusive contexts (Study 1) and completed dialogues (Study 2). Severe swears were rated most inappropriate regardless of context, Indian participants showed different norms, and women rated swearing less appropriate. It uses a mild/moderate/severe banding but appears to use English swearwords; the language of the stimuli was not confirmed. It is not a norm set for Indian-language words. The absence of human-rated norms for the seven Indian languages could not be confirmed or refuted, since it is an absence claim. Keep Low.

checked.claim: No Spanish taboo-word offensiveness norms; MADS (875 words, 540 native speakers, dominance, familiarity, AoA, sensory experience); Mexican Spanish ANEW found regional differences in arousal; RAE 'malsonante' and ASALE Diccionario de americanismos labels ('vulg.', 'desp.') are standard practice.
checked.source: Hinojosa, J. A., Rincón-Pérez, I., Romero-Ferreiro, M. V., et al. (2016). The Madrid Affective Database for Spanish (MADS): Ratings of dominance, familiarity, subjective age of acquisition and sensory experience. PLoS ONE, 11(5), e0155866. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0155866 (PMC4882010). Huerta-Chavez et al. (2025). Mexican Spanish adaptation for the ANEW. Behavior Research Methods, doi 10.3758/s13428-025-02703-5 (PMC12069142)
checked.correction: MADS confirmed: 875 words, 540 Spanish native speakers, dominance, familiarity, subjective AoA and sensory experience. Valence, arousal and discrete emotions are in the companion paper, Hinojosa et al. (2016), Behavior Research Methods 48, 272-284. Mexican ANEW: 2025, Huerta-Chavez, Llamas-Alonso and Angulo-Chavira, 753 participants, 1,028 words, SAM scale. Its abstract stresses culturally specific adaptation and gender differences. A specific finding of regional differences in arousal was NOT confirmed. A Rioplatense (Argentine) ANEW adaptation reports regional differences in general. The RAE 'malsonante' label and the ASALE 'vulg.'/'desp.' labels were not checked in this pass. Also note the Spain/Chile maricón/puto contrast from Sulpizio et al. (2024), the only Spanish offensiveness data confirmed.

claims.claim: Ofcom's 2016 research (Ipsos MORI) rated words in four tiers, mild / medium / strong / strongest, each with a pre-watershed acceptability gloss. Examples: 'cow' and 'crap' were mild ('generally of little concern'); 'feck'/'effing' medium ('potentially unacceptable pre-watershed'); 'cock' and 'flaps' strong ('generally unacceptable pre-watershed'); 'fuck' strongest ('unacceptable before the watershed'). Discriminatory language was treated separately and seen as more problematic than general swearing.
claims.source: Ofcom / Ipsos MORI (2016). Attitudes to potentially offensive language and gestures on TV and radio, and its Quick Reference Guide.
claims.population: UK adults, English L1 (plus minority-group participants)
claims.scale: mild / medium / strong / strongest
claims.relevance: This is the baseline scale. It has four ordinal levels anchored to a broadcast-time rule, and it suggests the app's 'level' field could be a 4-point ordinal. The PDF was blocked here, so the tier names and glosses come from search excerpts; one excerpt suggested the 2021 guide may say 'moderate' instead of 'medium'. Check the label against the PDF.

claims.claim: Method of the 2016 study: mixed methods with 248 participants from around the UK. It built on earlier Ofcom studies from 2005 and 2010, tested more words, and tested gestures for the first time. 'Discriminatory or racist words were the least acceptable categories of words', and context was 'one of the most important considerations', making isolated judgements of specific words difficult.
claims.source: Ofcom (2016). Attitudes to potentially offensive language and gestures on TV and radio (full report); Ipsos UK summary page.
claims.relevance: The ratings come from a small qualitative and deliberative sample, not a large norming survey. Ofcom itself warns that rating words outside their context is hard, which argues for a context note on each card alongside the level.

claims.claim: Ofcom's 2021 update (Ipsos MORI, published 22 September 2021) used a quantitative survey of 186 words. It ran 22-26 February 2021, with 368 respondents rating all 186 words (about 37 per day) for acceptability before and after the 9pm watershed. A qualitative strand of 37 online discussion groups and 25 depth interviews ran 15 February to 6 May 2021. The study also covered blackface, accent mimicry, misgendering and deadnaming.
claims.source: Ofcom / Ipsos MORI (2021). Public attitudes towards offensive language on TV and radio: Summary report and Quick Reference Guide.
claims.population: UK adults, English (some race and religion terms from other languages included)
claims.scale: Per-word acceptability before and after the watershed, published as tiered word ratings (tier labels not checked against the 2021 PDF)
claims.relevance: The scale is derived from crowd acceptability ratings tied to a time of day, which is a usable model for how the app's levels could be justified. The 2021 Quick Reference Guide has sections on race, nationality and ethnicity, which may include South Asian slurs relevant to the app's learners. That was not checked.

claims.claim: Ofcom's 2021 findings: audiences are more relaxed about most swearing, especially when accidental and quickly apologised for, but concern about discriminatory language, particularly about race, is increasing. Ofcom said the findings 'will not fundamentally change Ofcom's approach' but it would review its guidance.
claims.source: Ofcom (2021). News release and Note to Broadcasters on offensive language research.
claims.relevance: Supports keeping slurs separate from general swearing (a separate axis, or always-top severity), because attitudes to the two are moving in opposite directions.

claims.claim: The BBFC no longer uses a fixed list of swear words ranked by offence. It weighs the strength, context and tone of the words used, and rates language delivered in an 'aggressive, directed or sexual manner' higher than comedic or self-referential uses. The thresholds are: U 'very mild'; PG 'mild bad language only'; 12A/12 'infrequent use of strong language' (e.g. 'fuck'); 15 'frequent use of strong language' with the 'strongest terms (for example, 'cunt')' acceptable if justified by context; 18 no constraints on language. The current guidelines took effect 1 May 2024 after a 2023 consultation with 12,000 people, which found parental concern about terms with sexual or misogynistic connotations ('bitch', 'dick').
claims.source: BBFC (2024). Classification Guidelines; BBFC Guide: Language; BBFC education page 'Language'.
claims.scale: very mild / mild / strong / strongest (aligned to U / PG / 12A / 15 / 18)
claims.relevance: A second UK scale with a similar ordinal (very mild to strongest). It adds an explicit rule that delivery (aggressive or directed versus casual) raises severity, which could go in the card's usage note. The BBFC site was blocked here; quotes are from search excerpts of BBFC pages.

claims.claim: Australia's Guidelines for the Classification of Films and Computer Games (2012) use a six-step impact scale tied to the rating categories: 'very mild - G, mild - PG, moderate - M, strong - MA 15+, high - R 18+, and very high - RC'. Coarse language is judged on this impact scale, and impact 'may be lessened where reference to a classifiable element is verbal rather than visual'.
claims.source: Australian Government (2012). Guidelines for the Classification of Films / Computer Games 2012, F2012L01934.
claims.scale: very mild / mild / moderate / strong / high / very high
claims.relevance: The finest-grained official scale found. It also shows that regulators share common anchor words (mild, moderate, strong). The full text was not read; the scale comes from a search excerpt of the legislation PDF.

claims.claim: ACMA classification descriptors: G allows 'Very mild coarse language' only infrequently when absolutely justified; PG allows 'Mild or socially offensive coarse language ... infrequently'; at M 'coarse language is permitted but aggressive or strong coarse language should be infrequent'.
claims.source: ACMA classification descriptors as reproduced in MovieLabs 'AU ACMA Ratings' v2.4/2.5.
claims.relevance: Shows frequency and aggression as modifiers within a level, which are context rather than word properties. This is a secondary reproduction.

claims.claim: US FCC: there are no severity levels, only a binary. 'Profane' content is 'grossly offensive' language considered a public nuisance (older FCC text adds 'personally reviling epithets naturally tending to provoke violent resentment'). Indecent and profane content is barred on broadcast TV and radio from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; the 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. 'safe harbor' has applied since 1995. The FCC found a single live 'F-word' at the 2003 Golden Globes profane.
claims.source: FCC consumer guide 'Obscene, Indecent and Profane Broadcasts'; archived FCC pages (2004).
claims.scale: Binary: profane/indecent (restricted 6am-10pm) vs. not
claims.relevance: Not useful as a learner scale. It does show the US regulator treats slurs as 'reviling epithets', the same category as the strongest swearwords.

claims.claim: MPA (US film ratings): one use of 'one of the harsher sexually-derived words, though only as an expletive' starts a film at PG-13. Two or more uses, or one use in a sexual sense, mean R, unless the board votes by a two-thirds majority that PG-13 is still appropriate.
claims.source: MPA/CARA rating rules as reproduced by MovieLabs 'US MPAA Ratings' and TIME coverage.
claims.scale: Count-and-sense rules mapped to PG-13 / R
claims.relevance: Supports the user's 'needs extra care' idea: the same word changes severity depending on literal (sexual) versus expletive use, so cards could note sense-dependent severity.

claims.claim: ESRB (video games) has two language descriptors: 'Mild Language' ('Mild references to profanity, sexuality, violence, alcohol, or drug use') and 'Strong Language' ('Profanity and explicit references to sexuality, violence, alcohol, or drug use'). E10+ may contain mild language, T 'infrequent use of strong language', and M strong language.
claims.source: ESRB content descriptors as reproduced by Anime News Network and Plugged In (not esrb.org directly).
claims.scale: Mild Language / Strong Language
claims.relevance: A minimal two-level industry scale; too coarse for the app on its own.

claims.claim: India CBFC: the certification guidelines (1991, under the Cinematograph Act 1952 and Certification Rules 1983) say the Board shall ensure 'human sensibilities are not offended by vulgarity, obscenity or depravity' and that 'such dual meaning words as obviously cater to baser instincts are not allowed'. There is no graded language scale. A CBFC circular listing about 28 'objectionable and abusive' words to be cut was later 'put on hold'.
claims.source: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting reply in Parliament, reported by Indian Television; Rajya Sabha answer PQ 154 (23 May 1990).
claims.population: India, all film languages (Hindi and regional)
claims.scale: None (binary: allowed / cut), plus certificate U / UA / A
claims.relevance: India's regulator offers no levels to borrow. Its explicit ban on 'dual meaning words' is the closest regulatory parallel to the user's sound-alike warning. The 28-word list was not found.

claims.claim: The Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 2024 split UA into UA 7+, UA 13+ and UA 16+, and these age markers are advisory for parents. Per a secondary summary, A-certified films may contain 'abusive language' but not words that insult or degrade women, men or any social group. No published per-tier language thresholds were found.
claims.source: Press Information Bureau (2024). Government notifies the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 2024; Wikipedia 'Central Board of Film Certification'.
claims.scale: U / UA 7+ / UA 13+ / UA 16+ / A / S
claims.relevance: There are no Indian severity levels; slurs against groups are treated as beyond what even A allows, which matches putting slurs in a top 'never use' tier. The A-category language detail comes only from Wikipedia (Low to Medium).

claims.claim: India's Broadcasting Content Complaints Council (BCCC, set up by IBF/IBDF in June 2011) acts on complaints and issues advisories but has no graded word scale. In December 2012 it warned about comedy shows using 'crass, abusive, vulgar and double-meaning language with sexual overtones'; another advisory asked channels to avoid offensive language about SC/ST communities; in 2013 it fined Big CBS Spark Rs 2.5 lakh over offensive rap lyrics. It relies on the Programme Code (Rule 6, Cable Television Networks Rules 1994: content must not offend 'good taste or decency').
claims.source: exchange4media (2012, 2013) BCCC advisory and penalty reports; Caravan 'Table of Discontents'.
claims.scale: None (complaint-based, binary)
claims.relevance: Confirms there is no Indian levelled scale. It also flags caste-based slurs (SC/ST) as a sensitive class the app's Indian decks must cover, which has no direct UK equivalent.

gaps: WebFetch and curl were blocked (DNS failure or proxy 403 for ofcom.org.uk, bbfc.co.uk, ipsos.com), so no primary PDF was read in full. Every claim is Medium, from search-result excerpts of the primary pages. The tier labels and quotes should be checked against the PDFs before the app cites them.

Not checked: whether the 2021 Ofcom Quick Reference Guide keeps 'mild / medium / strong / strongest' or changes the wording (one excerpt suggested 'moderate'). Also not checked: which South Asian terms (e.g. 'P*ki') it rates and at what tier.
NBDSA (News Broadcasting & Digital Standards Authority) was not searched in depth; nothing found shows it grades language.
The CBFC's 28-word list and the September 2026 revised guidelines (one secondary mention) were not found; the language provisions of the 2024/2026 guidelines were not seen.

No regulator scale covers Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati, Assamese or Spanish swearwords. Levels for those words will need native-speaker rating, e.g. an Ofcom-style acceptability survey, or academic sources outside this angle.

No regulator offers a sound-alike (paronym) similarity scale. CBFC's ban on 'dual meaning words' is the only related concept found; the user's two similarity matrices will need linguistic or phonetic sources, not regulatory ones.
Spain's regulator (CNMC) and its age-rating codes for Spanish were not covered.

checked.claim: Ofcom 2016 (Ipsos MORI) four tiers mild / medium / strong / strongest with pre-watershed glosses; cow and crap mild, feck/effing medium, cock and flaps strong, fuck strongest; discriminatory language more problematic.
checked.source: Ofcom/Ipsos MORI (2016) Quick Reference Guide, https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0023/91625/OfcomQRG-AOC.pdf (search excerpts only; ofcom.org.uk blocked here). Secondary: Shortlist https://www.shortlist.com/news/ofcom-has-ranked-every-british-swear-word ; LADbible https://www.ladbible.com/entertainment/swear-words-english-language-strongest-weakest-20220131 ; Marie Claire https://www.marieclaire.co.uk/uncategorised/all-the-words-too-naughty-for-tv-ranked-by-offcom-in-order-of-rudeness-451749
checked.correction: Confidence stays Medium. Search excerpts of the Ofcom PDF confirm the tier names mild / medium / strong / strongest. They also confirm the glosses: 'generally of little concern' (mild); Feck/Effing 'medium language, potentially unacceptable pre-watershed'; Flaps 'strong language, generally unacceptable pre-watershed'; Fuck 'strongest language, unacceptable pre-watershed'. Cunt and motherfucker are 'strongest language, problematic for some even post-watershed'. Cow and crap (mild) and cock (strong) are confirmed only by secondary press (Shortlist, LADbible), not by the Ofcom text. Per Marie Claire, the strongest tier is mostly discriminatory slurs. 2021 labels are unresolved: one search excerpt said the 2021 guide uses Mild, Moderate and Strong groupings, but this was not seen in the PDF.

checked.source: Ofcom (2016) full report https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0022/91624/OfcomOffensiveLanguage.pdf ; Ipsos summary https://www.ipsos.com/en-uk/attitudes-potentially-offensive-language-tv-and-radio ; Church Times https://churchtimes.co.uk/articles/2016/7-october/news/uk/blasphemy-ok-before-watershed
checked.correction: The following were confirmed: 248 participants, the 2005 and 2010 predecessor studies, a larger word list, a broader range of minority-group participants, and gestures tested for the first time. The finding that discriminatory or racist terms were judged least acceptable was confirmed in paraphrase only. The exact quoted wording, and the phrase 'one of the most important considerations', were not seen verbatim. Item count: Church Times says 144 words and 6 gestures; Ipsos says 150 words and gestures in total.

checked.claim: Ofcom 2021 update (Ipsos MORI, 22 Sep 2021): 186 words, survey 22-26 Feb 2021, 368 respondents rating all 186 (about 37/day) before and after the watershed; 37 online groups and 25 depth interviews, 15 Feb to 6 May 2021; also blackface, accent mimicry, misgendering, deadnaming.
checked.source: Ofcom/Ipsos MORI (2021) https://www.ofcom.org.uk/research-and-data/tv-radio-and-on-demand/tv-research/offensive-language ; Ipsos https://www.ipsos.com/en-uk/public-attitudes-towards-offensive-language-tv-and-radio ; QRG https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0020/225335/offensive-language-quick-reference-guide.pdf
checked.correction: Every number and date was confirmed via search excerpts of the Ofcom and Ipsos pages. The QRG notes that respondents rated '186 English words in isolation, which many found difficult'. The 2021 tier labels are still unchecked.

checked.claim: Ofcom 2021: more relaxed about most swearing, especially accidental and quickly apologised; concern about discriminatory language (race) increasing; findings 'will not fundamentally change Ofcom's approach'; guidance to be reviewed.
checked.source: Ofcom Note to Broadcasters (22 Sep 2021) https://www.ofcom.org.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/225432/Note-to-Broadcasters-Offensive-Language-Research.pdf ; Ofcom news release https://www.ofcom.org.uk/news-centre/2021/public-attitudes-towards-offensive-language-on-tv-and-radio-revealed
checked.correction: The substance is confirmed, but the quote is not verbatim. The note says Ofcom 'does not consider that the findings of the new research will fundamentally change Ofcom's approach to applying the offensive language rules'. It commits to reviewing the guidance; licensees should use the existing guidance until then. A May 2022 note repeats this. The news release adds: 1% of 2020 complaints were about swearing and 8% about racial discrimination.

checked.claim: BBFC: no fixed ranked list; weighs strength, context, tone; aggressive/directed/sexual delivery rated higher. Thresholds U 'very mild', PG 'mild bad language only', 12A 'infrequent use of strong language', 15 'frequent use of strong language' with 'strongest terms (e.g. cunt)' if justified, 18 no constraints. 2024 guidelines effective 1 May 2024 after 2023 consultation of 12,000; concern about 'bitch', 'dick'.
checked.source: BBFC 'Our new classification guidelines are here' https://bbfc.co.uk/about-us/articles/our-new-classification-guidelines-are-here ; BBFC language page https://www.bbfc.co.uk/education/issues/language ; BBFC Guide to Language PDF (darkroom.bbfc.co.uk); BBFC Guidelines 2002 (Argyll & Bute mirror) https://www.argyll-bute.gov.uk/moderngov/documents/s13350/BBFCGuidelines2002.pdf
checked.correction: Confirmed: there is no fixed ranked list; strength, context and tone are weighed; delivery that is aggressive, directed or sexual can be rated higher than comedic or self-referential use. Also confirmed: about 12,000 people consulted in 2023, guidelines effective 1 May 2024, and parental concern about sexual or misogynistic terms ('son of a bitch', 'bitch', 'dick'). The threshold quotes are wrong for 2024. 'Infrequent use of strong language (eg fuck)' at 12A and 'frequent use of strong language... strongest terms (eg cunt) acceptable only where justified by context' at 15 are older (2002-era) wording. Secondary summaries give the 2024 wording as follows. 12A/12: 'moderate bad language, and strong language may be permitted, depending on context and frequency'. 15: 'strong language, and very strong language may be permitted depending on the context and frequency'. PG: 'mild bad language only'. The U wording was not confirmed. The current scale therefore reads roughly mild / moderate / strong / very strong. The BBFC site was blocked here.

checked.claim: Australia 2012 classification guidelines: impact hierarchy 'very mild - G, mild - PG, moderate - M, strong - MA 15+, high - R 18+, and very high - RC'; impact may be lessened where reference is verbal rather than visual. URL F2012L01934.
checked.source: Federal Register of Legislation: F2012L01934 (Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2012) https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/F2012L01934 ; F2012L02541 (Guidelines for the Classification of Films 2012) https://legislation.gov.au/F2012L02541/asmade/2012-12-19/text/original/pdf
checked.correction: The impact hierarchy and the verbal-versus-visual rule are confirmed in the 2012 Films Guidelines, and the hierarchy also appears in the 2005 edition. The citation is wrong, though. F2012L01934 is the Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2012, which were superseded on 22 September 2024 by F2023L01424. The Films guidelines are F2012L02541, made 19 December 2012 and commencing 1 January 2013. The two are separate instruments, not one 'Films and Computer Games' document.

checked.claim: ACMA descriptors: G 'Very mild coarse language' infrequent when absolutely justified; PG 'Mild or socially offensive coarse language ... infrequently'; M coarse language permitted but 'aggressive or strong coarse language should be infrequent'.
checked.source: MovieLabs AU ACMA Ratings v2.5 https://movielabs.com/md/ratings/v2.5/html/AU_ACMA_Ratings.html (search excerpt); Clickview staff guide https://whitefriars.libguides.com/Clickview/forstaff ; ACMA BI-492 https://acma.gov.au/sites/default/files/2019-09/BI-492.docx
checked.correction: The PG and M wording is confirmed via search excerpts of secondary reproductions. The G wording 'absolutely justified' was not seen; the 2012 guidelines say G language should be 'very mild and infrequent, and be justified by context'. ACMA decision BI-492 shows 'shit' and 'arse' accepted at PG, with 'fuck' beeped.

checked.claim: US FCC: binary, no levels; profane = 'grossly offensive' language considered a public nuisance (older text: 'personally reviling epithets naturally tending to provoke violent resentment'); indecent/profane barred 6am-10pm; safe harbor since 1995; 2003 Golden Globes F-word found profane.
checked.source: FCC consumer guide https://fcc.gov/consumers/guides/obscene-indecent-and-profane-broadcasts ; FCC Golden Globe order FCC 04-43 (March 2004) https://www.fcc.gov/eb/Orders/2004/FCC-04-43A1.html
checked.correction: Confirmed: 'grossly offensive' language considered a public nuisance; indecent and profane content barred from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; a 1995 D.C. Circuit remand leading to the 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. safe harbor. On the Golden Globes, the Commission order of March 2004 (FCC 04-43) reversed the Bureau and found Bono's 19 January 2003 utterance both indecent and profane under 18 U.S.C. 1464. No fine was imposed. The phrase 'personally reviling epithets naturally tending to provoke violent resentment' was not found in the sources checked. It derives from Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942); FCC use of it is unconfirmed. The claim that slurs are FCC 'reviling epithets' is therefore unsupported.

checked.claim: MPA: one use of a harsher sexually-derived word as an expletive starts at PG-13; more than one, or one in a sexual sense, is R unless two-thirds of the board vote for PG-13.
checked.source: MovieLabs US MPAA Ratings v2.4.4 https://movielabs.com/md/ratings/v2.4.4/html/US_MPAA_Ratings.html ; TIME newsfeed https://newsfeed.time.com/?p=90381 ; Rating System Wiki
checked.correction: Confirmed via search excerpts of secondary reproductions. The two-thirds vote rests on a finding that most American parents would consider PG-13 appropriate, because of context or because the use is inconspicuous.

checked.claim: ESRB: 'Mild Language' ('Mild references to profanity, sexuality, violence, alcohol, or drug use') and 'Strong Language' ('Profanity and explicit references to sexuality, violence, alcohol, or drug use'); E10+ mild language, T infrequent strong language, M strong language.

Source: Rajya Sabha PQ 154 (23 May 1990).

The December 2012 advisory was approved at the 20th meeting on 14 December 2012, with the quoted wording. claims.claim: HurtLex (Bassignana, Basile & Patti, 2018, 'Hurtlex: A Multilingual Lexicon of Words to Hurt', CLiC-it 2018, CEUR pp. 52-57) starts from Tullio De Mauro's Italian hate lexicon and was semi-automatically translated into over 50 languages. Each word gets one of 17 categories (e.g. PS ethnic slurs, DDF physical disabilities, DDP cognitive disabilities, ASM/ASF male/female genitalia, PR prostitution, OM homosexuality, CDS derogatory words, AN animals, RE crime/immoral conduct) plus a stereotype flag. Its only 'level' field is 'conservative' ('obtained by translating offensive senses of the words in the original lexicon') vs 'inclusive' ('obtained by translating all the potentially relevant senses'). That is translation confidence, not severity. The general lexicon has no per-word offensiveness score.
claims.source: Bassignana, Basile, Patti 2018, CLiC-it; HurtLex GitHub README
claims.population: Italian source lexicon; machine-translated versions include Hindi (HI), Bengali (BN), Spanish (ES). Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati and Assamese are not in the list.
claims.scale: category codes (17) + stereotype flag; level = conservative | inclusive
claims.relevance: Useful as a category taxonomy for tagging cards (what kind of insult: caste/ethnic, disability, sexual, animal, family). It gives no severity grade, and the Hindi and Bengali lists are machine-translated, so they cannot be trusted for card content.

claims.claim: HurtLex's README says only the Italian 'Revised HurtLex' has scores: 'every headword is annotated with an offensiveness level score'. Contributors may add 'a new column with a real value between 0 and 1'. The revised lexicon (Tontodimamma, Fontanella, Anzani & Basile, 2022, Quality & Quantity, DOI 10.1007/s11135-022-01494-7) got its per-word offensiveness score by fitting an Item Response Theory (graded response) model to ratings from many annotators. A follow-up compared 5-point Likert ratings with best-worst scaling.
claims.source: HurtLex README; Tontodimamma et al. 2022, Quality & Quantity (secondary summaries; full text not reachable)
claims.scale: continuous score (README: 0-1 column); annotators used a 5-point Likert scale (exact anchors not seen)
claims.relevance: The best model found for per-word grading: collect Likert ratings from native speakers, then calibrate. A small native-speaker rating round for each Fluenough language could reuse this method and then be binned into 4 Ofcom-style bands.

claims.claim: Sulpizio et al. (2024), 'Taboo language across the globe: A multi-lab study', Behavior Research Methods 56(4):3794-3813, DOI 10.3758/s13428-024-02376-6. Study 1 collected taboo words from community members (N = 1046). Study 2 had speakers rate them on six dimensions, including offensiveness, tabooness, valence and arousal (N = 455 per dimension), using best-worst scaling. It covers 13 languages and 17 countries, including Spain and Chile for Spanish. The authors report 'a significant amount of cross-country variability in words' tabooness and offensiveness'. Example: puto is similarly taboo in Chile and Spain but more offensive in Chile. Scores are standardized within each language, so they cannot be compared across languages.
claims.source: Sulpizio et al. 2024, Behavior Research Methods (open access, PMC11133054)
claims.population: L1 speakers in 17 countries; Spanish via Spain and Chile. No Indian language was seen in the country list (Australia, Belgium, Botswana, Canada, China, Chile, France, Germany, Finland, Italy, Serbia, Singapore, Slovenia, Spain, Thailand, UK, US).
claims.scale: best-worst scaling scores, standardized within language (exact anchors not read)
claims.relevance: Directly usable for Spanish: per-word offensiveness data for Spain and Chile. It also supports showing region on Spanish cards (Spain vs Latin America), because the same word grades differently by country.

claims.claim: SHARE (Plaza-del-Arco, Parras Portillo, López-Úbeda, Botella Gil & Martín-Valdivia, 2022, 'SHARE: A Lexicon of Harmful Expressions by Spanish Speakers', LREC 2022, pp. 1307-1316) holds 10,125 offensive terms and expressions that Spanish speakers gave to a Telegram chatbot ('Fiero'). Five annotators labeled them manually, with kappa 78.8%. The summaries found describe labels and categories but no per-term severity grade.
claims.source: Plaza-del-Arco et al. 2022, LREC
claims.scale: labels only (no severity scale found)
claims.relevance: A large, human-sourced Spanish insult inventory to draw card candidates from. Severity would still need to come from Sulpizio et al. or a rating round.

claims.claim: OffendES (Plaza-del-Arco et al., RANLP 2021, 'OffendES: A New Corpus in Spanish for Offensive Language Research') labels 47,128 Spanish social-media comments (30,416 released) with four classes: OFP (offensive, target a person), OFG (offensive, target a group), NOE ('non-offensive but with expletive language': 'rude words, blasphemes, or swearwords but without the aim of offending, and usually with a positive connotation') and NO (non-offensive). A subset attaches a confidence degree to each label.
claims.source: Plaza-del-Arco et al. 2021, RANLP; SINAI/OffendES Hugging Face card
claims.population: Spanish (Spain), comments on young influencers' posts
claims.scale: OFP / OFG / NOE / NO (comment-level, not per-word)
claims.relevance: The NOE class backs a separate card field: 'can be friendly or neutral among peers' vs 'aimed to hurt'. Learners need this alongside severity.

claims.claim: HASOC labels are post-level only, with no severity ranking. Mandl, Modha et al. (2019), 'Overview of the HASOC track at FIRE 2019' (FIRE 2019, DOI 10.1145/3368567.3368584; CEUR Vol-2517 T3-1) covered Hindi, German and English. Modha et al. (2021), 'Overview of the HASOC Subtrack at FIRE 2021', covered English, Hindi and Marathi Twitter data. Task A is binary, HOF vs NOT. Task B (English and Hindi only) splits HOF into HATE, OFFENSIVE and PROFANITY. Marathi has only the binary task (1874 training items). HASOC 2023 Task 4 (Assamese, Bengali, Bodo) is also binary, HOF vs NOT; Gujarati was in another 2023 task.
claims.source: Modha/Mandl et al. HASOC overviews 2019, 2021, 2023 (abstracts and secondary summaries)
claims.population: Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Assamese, Gujarati (plus English, German, Bodo); social media, L1 users
claims.scale: HOF / NOT; fine-grained HATE / OFFN / PRFN (2019 label strings from memory, not verified)
claims.relevance: Shows that the main Indic resources give offensive/not labels only, so they cannot supply per-word levels. HATE vs PROFANITY is still a useful card tag.

claims.claim: The DravidianLangTech-EACL 2021 offensive language shared task (Chakravarthi et al.; see 'Developing Successful Shared Tasks on Offensive Language Identification for Dravidian Languages', arXiv 2111.03375) labels code-mixed YouTube comments in Tamil (over 30k), Malayalam (over 20k) and Kannada (about 8k) with 6 classes: Not Offensive, Offensive Untargeted, Offensive Targeted Individual, Offensive Targeted Group, Offensive Targeted Other, and Not in intended language. HOLD-Telugu (DravidianLangTech 2024) did hate/offensive detection on Telugu code-mixed YouTube comments.
claims.source: DravidianLangTech 2021 and 2024 shared-task papers (secondary summaries)
claims.population: Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu; code-mixed social media
claims.scale: 6-class target labels (no severity)
claims.relevance: Kannada and Telugu resources exist, but they label targets, not severity, so they cannot set per-word levels.

claims.claim: BD-SHS (Romim et al., LREC 2022, 'BD-SHS: A Benchmark Dataset for Learning to Detect Online Bangla Hate Speech in Different Social Contexts') has 50,281 Bengali comments with three label levels: hate vs not; target (individual, male, female, group); type (slander, religion, gender, call to violence). The earlier HS-BAN (Romim et al. 2021) is binary.
claims.source: Romim et al. 2022, LREC; arXiv 2206.00372
claims.scale: binary + target + type labels (no severity)
claims.relevance: Bengali type tags (religion, gender, slander) match HurtLex-style categories. They give no per-word level.

claims.claim: MACD (Gupta et al., NeurIPS 2022 Datasets and Benchmarks, 'Multilingual Abusive Comment Detection at Scale for Indic Languages') has 150K ShareChat/Moj comments in 5 Indic languages (Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil and Telugu appear in the related Moj tables), about 49% abusive. Labels are binary, abusive vs non-abusive.
claims.source: Gupta et al. 2022, NeurIPS (abstract via search summary)
claims.scale: binary
claims.relevance: Another large Indic resource with no per-word severity. It is a source of real attested words to check, not of levels.

claims.claim: Dewaele (2004), 'The emotional force of swearwords and taboo words in the speech of multilinguals', Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development 25:204-222, surveyed 1039 multilinguals. It found that 'the perceived emotional force of S-T words is highest in the L1 and gradually lower in languages learned subsequently'. Instructed learners rated force lower than naturalistic learners.
claims.source: Dewaele 2004, JMMD (abstract)
claims.population: Multilingual adults, L1 vs L2/L3+ (web questionnaire)
claims.scale: self-rated emotional force (format not read)
claims.relevance: The core reason for the deck: classroom L2 learners underrate how strong these words are. Levels must come from L1 speakers' judgments, and cards should say plainly that a word feels stronger to native ears than it will to the learner.

claims.claim: No published Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati or Assamese lexicon with per-word offensiveness or severity ratings was found. Searches turned up only popular guides and a 2025 Asian Englishes corpus study of Hindi-derived swearwords on Reddit ('Bad' Indian English, TU Dresden), which looks at semantic fields, not severity.
claims.source: Search outcome (negative finding)
claims.scale: none found
claims.relevance: The app needs its own grading for the Indic decks. Best practice from the sources: an Ofcom-like 4-band scale (mild / medium / strong / strongest), set by several native-speaker raters per language using a Likert or best-worst method (as in Tontodimamma 2022 and Sulpizio 2024), plus HurtLex-style category tags and a region note.

gaps: Could not open full texts (Springer, PMC, arXiv, iris.unito, ISCTE were unreachable), so the exact scale anchors are unverified for Sulpizio 2024 (best-worst offensiveness), Tontodimamma 2022 (Likert points, score range) and Dewaele 2004.
Full 13-language list of Sulpizio 2024 not confirmed. No Indian language was seen.
HASOC 2019 fine-grained label strings (HATE/OFFN/PRFN, TIN/UNT) are from memory, not verified in the paper.
No resource found for Assamese or Gujarati offensive words beyond HASOC 2023 binary labels, and none for per-word severity in any Indic language.

No research found on near-homophones or similar-sounding innocent words in Indian languages or Spanish (the user's 'similarity matrix' request). The app will have to build both similarity lists (sound-alike and spelling-alike) itself, e.g. by edit distance over ISO 15919/IPA transcriptions, and have native speakers review them.
SHARE's exact label set (whether it includes any intensity field) was not read from the paper.

checked.claim: HurtLex (Bassignana, Basile & Patti 2018, CLiC-it 2018): De Mauro source lexicon, 17 categories + stereotype, level = conservative vs inclusive (translation of senses, not severity), >50 languages incl. HI, BN, ES but not TE/MR/KN/GU/AS; no per-word score in general lexicon.
checked.source: HurtLex GitHub README (read directly: https://github.com/valeriobasile/hurtlex); CLiC-it 2018 record, CEUR Vol-2253 (search summary)
checked.correction: README read directly. It confirms the category codes (PS, RCI, PA, DDF, DDP, DMC, IS, OR, AN, ASM, ASF, PR, OM, QAS, CDS, RE, SVP) and the exact conservative/inclusive definitions. The 53-language list includes Hindi, Bengali and Spanish but not Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati or Assamese. Search confirmed the De Mauro source ('Le Parole per Ferire'), the 17 categories and semi-automatic translation into 'more than 50 languages' in CEUR Vol-2253. I could not reach CEUR (proxy blocked), so the page range 52-57 is unverified.

checked.claim: Revised HurtLex (Italian) has a per-word offensiveness score; README asks contributors for a 0-1 column; Tontodimamma, Fontanella, Anzani & Basile 2022, Quality & Quantity, DOI 10.1007/s11135-022-01494-7, IRT (graded response) on many annotators' ratings; follow-up compared 5-point Likert with best-worst scaling.
checked.source: HurtLex README (read directly); Tontodimamma et al., 'An Italian lexical resource for incivility detection in online discourses', Quality & Quantity (search summary, iris.unito.it PDF not reachable); Tontodimamma, Anzani & Fontanella 2022, 'Comparison of two annotation schemes to derive offensiveness scores in HurtLex' (ricerca.unich.it/handle/11564/795972, abstract via search)

Add the Q&Q paper's title, 'An Italian lexical resource for incivility detection in online discourses'. It was accepted on 5 July 2022, and one listing dates it 2023. The 'graded response' detail is confirmed by the companion paper's abstract, not the Q&Q abstract: 5-point Likert per word, then a unidimensional Graded Response Model, compared with best-worst scaling. That companion paper is by Tontodimamma, Anzani & Fontanella (without Basile). Confidence stays Medium.

checked.claim: Sulpizio et al. 2024, 'Taboo language across the globe: A multi-lab study', Behav Res Methods 56(4):3794-3813, DOI 10.3758/s13428-024-02376-6; Study 1 N=1046, Study 2 N=455 per dimension, six dimensions, best-worst scaling, 13 languages / 17 countries incl. Spain and Chile; 'a significant amount of cross-country variability in words' tabooness and offensiveness'; puto example; within-language standardized scores.
checked.source: Sulpizio et al. 2024 abstract via repository records (repositorio.iscte-iul.pt/handle/10071/32818, boa.unimib.it/handle/10281/511279); Springer/PMC full text not reachable
checked.correction: Confirmed from abstracts: citation, volume, issue and pages; Study 1 N = 1046; Study 2 N = 455 raters for each of six dimensions; 13 languages and 17 countries on five continents; the exact cross-country variability quote. Best-worst scaling appears among the keywords, but I could not confirm it was the method for every dimension. Search confirms Botswana, Canada, Chile, Serbia, Singapore, Slovenia and Thailand among the countries. I could NOT verify the 'puto' Chile-vs-Spain example, that scores are standardized within each language, or the full 17-country list (Spain included). Drop the puto example and the standardization claim, or mark them unverified, until someone reads the full text.

checked.claim: SHARE (Plaza-del-Arco et al. 2022, LREC, pp. 1307-1316): 10,125 offensive terms/expressions from Spanish speakers via Telegram chatbot Fiero; five annotators, kappa 78.8%; no per-term severity grade.
checked.source: Plaza-del-Arco et al. 2022, LREC (aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.139, abstract via search); SINAI resource page (sinai.ujaen.es/en/research/resources/share-lexicon-harmful-expressions-spanish-population)
checked.correction: Confirmed: pages 1307-1316, 10,125 terms, the Fiero Telegram chatbot, five annotators and kappa 78.8%. The SINAI page breaks the terms down as 5,888 unigrams, 2,447 bigrams and 1,790 trigrams, and says the lexicon is free for research only, with no redistribution. That licence matters before using it as a source for app content. I found no severity scale, but did not read the full text.

checked.claim: OffendES (Plaza-del-Arco et al., RANLP 2021): 47,128 Spanish comments (30,416 released), four classes OFP/OFG/NOE/NO, NOE definition, subset with confidence degree.
checked.source: OffendES abstract via search (aclanthology.org/2021.ranlp-1.123); ODESIA task page (portal.odesia.uned.es); MeOffendEs@IberLEF 2021 CodaLab page
checked.correction: Confirmed: 47,128 comments on young influencers' posts (Twitter, Instagram, YouTube), manually labeled; a subset carries a confidence degree per label; RANLP 2021 pp. 1096-1108. The NOE definition matches: 'rude words, blasphemes, or swearwords' without aim to offend, 'usually with a positive connotation'. Correction: the scheme has a fifth class, OFO (offensive, target is neither a person nor a group), per ODESIA, though the shared-task page speaks of four. I could not verify the 30,416 released figure (Hugging Face not reachable).

checked.claim: HASOC: 2019 overview (Hindi, German, English); 2021 overview (English, Hindi, Marathi Twitter); Task A binary HOF/NOT; Task B (English and Hindi only) HATE/OFFENSIVE/PROFANITY; Marathi binary only with 1874 training items; HASOC 2023 Task 4 (Assamese, Bengali, Bodo) binary; Gujarati in a separate 2023 task.
checked.source: Mandl/Modha et al. HASOC 2019 overview (FIRE 2019; CEUR Vol-2517 T3-1); HASOC 2021 overview (arXiv 2112.09301); HASOC 2023 Task 4 and Sinhala/Gujarati papers (CEUR Vol-3681); Marathi participant papers (e.g. arXiv 2110.12687)
checked.correction: Every structural claim is confirmed by abstracts or secondary sources. The Marathi training set is 1,874 tweets (1,205 NOT, 669 HOF). The 2023 Task 4 data are YouTube and Facebook comments labeled hate or non-hate. Gujarati was in the 2023 Sinhala/Gujarati subtrack (about 1,020 tweets). Participant papers give the label strings HATE / OFFN / PRFN (secondary sources only). The 2019 data was Twitter and Facebook. The Vol-2517 PDF itself was not reachable.

checked.claim: DravidianLangTech-EACL 2021 offensive task: code-mixed YouTube comments, Tamil >30k, Malayalam >20k, Kannada ~8k, 6 classes; HOLD-Telugu (DravidianLangTech 2024) on Telugu code-mixed YouTube comments.
checked.source: Chakravarthi et al., arXiv 2111.03375; participant papers (arXiv 2102.01051); CodaLab competition 27654; HOLD-Telugu findings paper, 2024.dravidianlangtech-1.8, pp. 49-55 (Premjith B et al.)
checked.correction: Sizes: Tamil 43,919, Malayalam 20,010, Kannada 7,772, so 'over 30k' for Tamil is an understatement. The labels are Not_offensive, Offensive_Untargeted, Offensive_Targeted_Insult_Individual / _Group / _Other, and not-{language}. The Malayalam training set has no 'Other' examples. HOLD-Telugu is confirmed: manually annotated Telugu code-mixed YouTube comments, 23 teams, macro F1. Its label scheme was not read.

checked.claim: BD-SHS (Romim et al., LREC 2022): 50,281 Bengali comments, three levels (hate/not; target individual/male/female/group; type slander/religion/gender/call to violence); earlier HS-BAN binary.
checked.source: Romim et al. 2022, arXiv 2206.00372 / aclanthology 2022.lrec-1.552 (abstract and Kaggle release via search); HS-BAN arXiv 2112.01902
checked.correction: Confirmed: 50,281 comments, 24,156 of them hate speech; the three-level scheme; the target and type categories as stated. The abstract's own wording is 'more than 50,200'. HS-BAN is confirmed as binary: more than 50,000 comments, 40.17% hate.

checked.claim: MACD (Gupta et al., NeurIPS 2022 Datasets and Benchmarks): ~150K ShareChat comments, 5 Indic languages, ~49% abusive, binary labels.
checked.source: Gupta et al. 2022, NeurIPS D&B abstract (proceedings.neurips.cc ... a7c4163b33286261b24c72fd3d1707c9-Abstract.html) via search
checked.correction: Confirmed: about 150K human-annotated ShareChat comments from about 70K users, 49% abusive, binary labels. The 5 languages are Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada, as listed for MACD itself, not just in 'related Moj tables'. Do not conflate it with MACI, a separate 665K Moj dataset from the IEEE BigMM challenge. MACD's source is ShareChat, not 'ShareChat/Moj'.

checked.claim: Dewaele (2004), JMMD 25:204-222, 1039 multilinguals; 'the perceived emotional force of S-T words is highest in the L1 and gradually lower in languages learned subsequently'; instructed learners rated force lower than naturalistic learners.
checked.source: Dewaele 2004 abstract (YorkSpace record via search: yorkspace.library.yorku.ca/items/9bd0b9a4-bfe8-44f3-92af-b0a2e4fc975d)
checked.correction: Search confirms the quote is in the abstract ('t-Tests revealed that ...'), along with N = 1039 and the web questionnaire. Naturalistic or partly naturalistic learners gave higher ratings than instructed learners. Citation is 25(2/3): 204-222, though one reference gives 204-223. I could not open YorkSpace directly (DNS blocked), so confidence is High from the search-quoted abstract.

checked.claim: No published per-word offensiveness/severity lexicon found for Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati or Assamese; only popular guides and a 2025 Asian Englishes corpus study of Hindi-derived swearwords on Reddit (TU Dresden) on semantic fields, not severity.
checked.source: Search outcome; 'Bad' Indian English on Reddit, Asian Englishes 27(3):783-800 (TU Dresden portal)
checked.correction: The TU Dresden article exists: Asian Englishes 27(3):783-800, online 2 September 2025, linked to Leuckert & Lange. Its abstract describes 'the forms, functions, and contexts' of madarchod, bhenchod and Indian-adapted 'fucker', using r/indianews and r/IndiaSpeaks. 'Semantic fields' is not the abstract's wording. It still gives no severity ratings. My searches also found no Indic per-word severity lexicon, but a negative finding stays Low confidence. Note also that HurtLex has machine-translated HI and BN lists, which are unscored.
